Human brains can have around 10 to the 10 neurons.

These are chemical signals that neurons
turn into electrical ones.

is some influx of ions from outside
on the synaptic cleft to the inside, which
is the sum of the neuron.
Eventually, the sum of the neuron
starts from the dendrites.
And this influx happens through receptors,
the gates that essentially open at different times.
And the first computational model
that actually described these dynamics,
these receptor dynamics in detail,
was the famous Hodgkin-Huxley model.

implement it in Neuroblox.
And another success of this model
is essentially because of the way
that [INAUDIBLE] were laid out, yes, it did

So this is a nice--
both abstract but also more practical at the same time
representation of this computational model.
So in more detail, the plasty--
synaptic-- sorry-- transmission, as I said,
this is a chemical signal.
We have synaptic vesicles being packaged
on the presynaptic side, and then
they get emitted in the synaptic cleft,
and they are picked up by receptors
on the postsynaptic neuron, which, consequently,
the receptors actually open the ion channels,
and we have the ion influx that actually causes
the postsynaptic potential because the influx actually
potentiates the neuron.
And people have observed these two types
of neurons we call integrators in class I
and resonators, class II.
So we can distinguish them by their fi-curve, which
is the firing-rate frequency over the injected current
to the neuron.
So we have neurons that actually,
as you inject more and more current,
the firing rate goes up almost proportionally
to the injected current.
But also, we have the resonators,
which, you can think of--
they function almost like a switch.
So up to some specific input current level, nothing happens.
There's no firing.
And then there is a jump to some firing
rate, which might grow proportionally afterwards
for higher values.
And here on the right, I just wanted
to show you essentially some face portraits
of how this is possible.

Right, moving on to the second category,
these are the neural mass models.
So you can think of neural mass models as a step
up on the abstraction ladder.
Such models were designed to capture,
on average, the activity of neurons or neurons
connected to one another.
And in general, they are oscillators or collections
of oscillators.
And here, you can see an example of that, which
is the [INAUDIBLE] oscillator.
So these are very much phenomenological models,
as in they don't rely on biology.
They just imitate this periodicity
in spiking, right, but in very simple terms.
So they just assume this sinusoid spiking,
and you have a pool of them.
But the handy thing about the [INAUDIBLE] oscillators,
as you can see in the diagram, is
that given a pool of oscillators,
you can, by changing this one variable in the model,
you can move from regimes of all of the oscillators oscillating
in a similar frequency so now you have synchronicity
to regimes where oscillators are more uniformly scattered,
and there is no synchronicity, or they're
split into different clusters.
So you have some flexibility in this model.

So the final section that I wanted to talk about
is our sources and specifically deep brain stimulation.
So deep brain stimulation is a neurosurgical procedure.
It has been applied--
I think one classic application of it
is Parkinson's disease to reduce motor symptoms like tremor
and rigidity.
The benefits of it is that it is adjustable and reversible.
And also, it allows thus for better medication management.
But also, now it has been extended,
and other brain disorders can also be treated with DBS.
So as I was saying, this is very much a real world application,
and we're trying to match exactly those real world
protocols in Neuroblox.
